what_it_does: Intel SGX (Software Guard Extensions) is a hardware feature that creates a walled-off, encrypted region of memory — called an 'enclave' — where sensitive code can run even if the operating system is compromised. A known class of attack called 'side-channel' leaks secret information not by breaking encryption but by watching indirect clues like timing differences. Software developers have tried to defend against this by writing 'balanced' branches — making both the 'yes' and 'no' paths of every if-statement take the same number of instructions and memory accesses, so there is nothing for a timing spy to observe. This paper discovers a new spy: the Memory Disambiguation Unit (MDU), a small circuit inside the CPU that tries to guess whether an upcoming memory load might conflict with a pending store. By watching how this unit's predictions change depending on what is happening inside the enclave, an attacker running on the same machine can extract secret information even when the software branches are perfectly balanced. The authors reverse-engineer how the MDU works on real Intel chips and demonstrate a complete end-to-end leak from an SGX enclave.
